triage.name: Renal tubular acidosis
triage.reason: Non-anion-gap metabolic acidosis with characteristic electrolyte patterns; a good acid-base reasoning case worked out from labs and history.

demographics: Primary (inherited) forms often present in infancy or childhood
Secondary forms are more often diagnosed in adults, especially women with autoimmune disease
Type 1 (distal) is the most common form overall

risk_factors.text: Family history of renal tubular acidosis or inherited tubulopathy
Autoimmune disease such as Sjögren syndrome, lupus or rheumatoid arthritis
Chronic use of a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor (acetazolamide, topiramate)
Chronic kidney disease or tubulointerstitial kidney disease

family_history: Renal tubular acidosis in a parent or sibling
Inherited tubulopathy or hearing loss in the family

chief_complaints.text: I feel weak and tired all the time
My muscles feel weak and I get cramps
I've been so thirsty and I'm peeing all the time
My child seems to be growing slowly and has bow legs

hpi.onset: Gradual over weeks to months; in inherited forms it can begin in infancy or early childhood
hpi.duration: Chronic, often present for months before diagnosis
hpi.progression: Slowly progressive; symptoms worsen as the acidosis and potassium loss continue, and can be intermittent in milder forms
hpi.location: Generalized; bone pain often in the back, hips and legs
hpi.quality: Constant tiredness and muscle weakness, with intermittent cramps; bone pain is dull and aching
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate at first, becoming more limiting with severe hypokalemia or advanced bone disease
hpi.timing: Continuous, often worse with activity or after a high-acid meal

associated_symptoms.text: Pins and needles in the hands and feet
Rickets or bowing of the legs in children

pertinent_negatives: Chronic alcohol use with poor intake
Ingestion of methanol, ethylene glycol or salicylates
Family history of recurrent kidney failure in childhood

argues_against: Profuse watery diarrhea causing bicarbonate loss
Colicky flank pain radiating to the groin

atypical.how_it_differs: Infants and young children present with failure to thrive, poor growth, vomiting, dehydration and rickets rather than the adult pattern of stones and muscle weakness.
Symptoms are often attributed to aging; bone pain and fractures may dominate, and mild acidosis can be an incidental lab finding.
Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy can mimic the acidosis symptoms, and the condition may first be noticed on routine blood work.
In chronic kidney disease the acidosis is often milder and the potassium may be high rather than low, so weakness and cramps are less prominent.

general.mild: Alert and comfortable at rest; no obvious distress
general.moderate: Tired-appearing, prefers to sit; mild muscle weakness on effort
general.severe: Ill-appearing, visibly weak, needs help moving; may be dehydrated
general.critical: Lethargic or obtunded, profound weakness, poor perfusion

findings.maneuver: Test strength against resistance in the proximal arms and legs, and ask the patient to rise from a chair
findings.finding: Symmetric proximal muscle weakness, worse with severe hypokalemia

findings.maneuver: Test the deep tendon reflexes at the biceps, knees and ankles
findings.finding: Reduced or absent deep tendon reflexes

findings.maneuver: Palpate the long bones, ribs and spine, and percuss the spine
findings.finding: Bone tenderness over the spine, hips or long bones

findings.maneuver: With the child standing, inspect the legs and measure the intercondylar distance
findings.finding: Bowing of the legs (genu varum) in a child with rickets

findings.maneuver: Plot height and weight on the growth chart and compare with prior measurements
findings.finding: Height and weight below the expected percentile for age

findings.maneuver: Inspect the oral mucosa and tongue
Palpate the parotid glands in front of and below the ears
findings.finding: Bilateral parotid gland enlargement suggesting Sjögren syndrome
Costovertebral angle tenderness suggesting stones or pyelonephritis

findings.maneuver: Palpate the abdomen and check for rebound tenderness
findings.finding: Abdomen soft, non-tender, without guarding or rebound

findings.maneuver: Press the pretibial area and inspect the ankles
Inspect the internal jugular vein at 45 degrees

labs.caveat: Low bicarbonate with a normal anion gap is the core finding; the value is what defines severity.
Hyperchloremia is what keeps the anion gap normal.
Hypokalemia is typical of type 1 and type 2; in type 4 the potassium is high instead.
Arterial or venous blood gas; a normal pH with low bicarbonate suggests a mixed disorder.
Respiratory compensation; a PaCO2 that is not appropriately low points to a second respiratory acidosis.
A urine pH above 5.5 despite systemic acidosis is the hallmark of distal (type 1) RTA; in proximal RTA the urine can acidify normally once the bicarbonate is very low.
Low specific gravity reflects the concentrating defect and polyuria.
Microscopic hematuria from stones or nephrocalcinosis.
Hypophosphatemia is prominent in proximal (type 2) RTA and contributes to rickets and osteomalacia.
Mild hypocalcemia can accompany the bone disease; correct for albumin.
Elevated with rickets or osteomalacia from chronic acidosis and phosphate loss.
Often normal early; a rising creatinine suggests chronic kidney disease or nephrocalcinosis rather than isolated tubular disease.
Low albumin with an autoimmune cause such as lupus; needed to interpret total calcium.

findings.finding: Ventricular tachycardia or torsades de pointes

imaging.preferred_when: First-line for suspected stones or nephrocalcinosis, and in children and pregnancy

findings.text: Increased echogenicity of the renal medullary pyramids (nephrocalcinosis)
Echogenic foci with shadowing in the collecting system (stones)

imaging.study: CT abdomen and pelvis without contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Suspected stone when ultrasound is nondiagnostic

imaging.study: Skeletal survey or bilateral knee and wrist radiographs
imaging.preferred_when: Children with growth failure or suspected rickets

findings.text: Cupping and splaying of the growth plate
Bowing deformity of the long bones

imaging.preferred_when: Adults with chronic acidosis and suspected bone loss

findings.text: Reduced bone mineral density (osteopenia or osteoporosis)

initial.why: Shows the non-anion-gap metabolic acidosis with low bicarbonate and high chloride, plus the potassium level
Confirms the acidosis and shows whether respiratory compensation is appropriate
Urine pH above 5.5 during acidosis points to distal RTA; also screens for stones and infection

initial.only_if: stones, hematuria or a history of nephrolithiasis are present

confirmatory.why: A positive urine anion gap during acidosis indicates impaired distal ammonium excretion (distal RTA)

confirmatory.test: Urine pH after ammonium chloride loading
confirmatory.why: Fails to fall below 5.5 in distal RTA; used when the diagnosis is uncertain
confirmatory.only_if: baseline urine pH is equivocal and the diagnosis remains unclear

confirmatory.test: Fractional excretion of bicarbonate after bicarbonate loading
confirmatory.why: Above 15% indicates proximal (type 2) RTA; below 5% indicates distal (type 1) RTA
confirmatory.only_if: the type of RTA is unclear from the initial workup

supporting.why: Assesses albumin, liver enzymes and total protein for an underlying systemic or autoimmune disorder
Hypomagnesemia can accompany and worsen the potassium wasting
Thyroid disease can cause weakness and electrolyte disturbance
Screens for adrenal insufficiency when hyperkalemia and acidosis suggest type 4 RTA

supporting.test: Skeletal survey or bilateral knee and wrist radiographs
supporting.why: Documents rickets in a child with growth failure
supporting.only_if: the patient is a child with poor growth or bone deformity

supporting.why: Assesses bone loss in adults with chronic acidosis
supporting.only_if: chronic acidosis or fragility fracture is present

not_indicated.why: Not needed unless there is a separate concern for lactic acidosis or hypoperfusion
Ketones are not the cause of a normal-anion-gap acidosis
No role unless abdominal pain suggests pancreatitis
No role in the evaluation of a metabolic acidosis

not_indicated.test: CT abdomen and pelvis without contrast
not_indicated.why: Reserved for suspected stones when ultrasound is nondiagnostic
not_indicated.only_if: a stone is suspected and ultrasound is inconclusive

decision_points: Confirm a normal anion gap before attributing the acidosis to a renal tubular cause
Check urine pH during the acidosis; a value above 5.5 favors distal RTA
Distinguish proximal from distal RTA with the urine anion gap and, if needed, bicarbonate loading
Check potassium: low in types 1 and 2, high in type 4
Screen for an underlying autoimmune disease, especially Sjögren syndrome, in adults

criteria.name: Diagnosis of renal tubular acidosis
criteria.summary: A normal-anion-gap (hyperchloremic) metabolic acidosis with an inappropriately alkaline urine and impaired renal acid excretion, in the absence of advanced kidney failure or a non-renal cause of bicarbonate loss such as diarrhea.
items: Low serum bicarbonate with a normal anion gap
Urine pH above 5.5 during systemic acidosis (distal type)
Positive urine anion gap or failure to acidify urine after an acid load
Fractional bicarbonate excretion above 15% after loading (proximal type)

differential.name: Diarrhea-induced bicarbonate loss
differential.why_considered: Profuse watery diarrhea causes a normal-anion-gap metabolic acidosis with hypokalemia, mimicking RTA
differential.trigger: Profuse watery diarrhea or laxative use before the acidosis

history: Profuse watery diarrhea or laxative misuse

differential.name: Diabetic ketoacidosis
differential.why_considered: Metabolic acidosis with weakness, polyuria and polydipsia, and can be confused with RTA before the anion gap is checked
differential.trigger: Hyperglycemia with ketones and a high anion gap

history: Known diabetes or new polyuria and weight loss
No chronic bone pain or stones

differential.name: Chronic kidney disease with metabolic acidosis
differential.why_considered: Failing kidneys cause a non-anion-gap acidosis with hyperkalemia and can look like type 4 RTA

exam: Volume overload, edema or uremic signs

differential.name: Primary hyperparathyroidism
differential.why_considered: Causes hypercalciuria, kidney stones and bone pain, overlapping with RTA

history: No muscle weakness or polyuria from hypokalemia

differential.name: Vitamin D deficiency rickets
differential.why_considered: Causes bow legs, growth failure and bone pain in children, similar to RTA-related rickets

imaging: Rachitic changes on wrist and knee radiographs

differential.name: Bartter syndrome
differential.why_considered: Causes hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis and polyuria, which can be confused with RTA if the acid-base status is not carefully reviewed

severity.mild: Mild acidosis (bicarbonate 18–21 mmol/L) with few or no symptoms; often found incidentally on labs
severity.moderate: Bicarbonate 14–18 mmol/L with fatigue, muscle weakness, cramps, polyuria and thirst; may have stones or bone pain
severity.severe: Bicarbonate 8–14 mmol/L with marked weakness, hyporeflexia, bone disease, nephrocalcinosis and growth failure in children
severity.critical: Bicarbonate below 8–10 mmol/L with profound hypokalemia, cardiac arrhythmias, paralysis or respiratory compromise

red_flags.meaning: Risk of cardiac arrhythmia, rhabdomyolysis and paralysis; needs urgent potassium replacement

red_flags.finding: ECG showing flattened T waves, U waves or prolonged QT
red_flags.meaning: Hypokalemic cardiac instability; monitor and replace potassium

red_flags.finding: Bicarbonate below 10 mmol/L with lethargy or confusion
red_flags.meaning: Severe metabolic acidosis; consider bicarbonate therapy and urgent evaluation

red_flags.finding: New muscle paralysis or respiratory weakness
red_flags.meaning: Severe hypokalemia or acidosis affecting neuromuscular function; emergency

red_flags.finding: Growth failure or bowing in a child
red_flags.meaning: Chronic acidosis causing rickets; needs prompt treatment to prevent permanent deformity

complications.name: Nephrolithiasis
clues: Colicky flank pain radiating to the groin

complications.name: Nephrocalcinosis
clues: Medullary calcifications on ultrasound or CT

complications.name: Rickets and osteomalacia
clues: Bowing of the legs in children

complications.name: Growth failure in children
clues: Height and weight below expected percentiles

complications.name: Severe hypokalemia with arrhythmia or paralysis

special_populations.differences: Often present with failure to thrive, vomiting, dehydration and rickets rather than stones; growth failure is a key clue and treatment must start early to prevent permanent deformity.
Symptoms may be attributed to aging; bone pain, fractures and incidental lab findings dominate, and mild acidosis is easily missed.
Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy can mimic symptoms; the condition may first be noticed on routine blood work, and potassium and bicarbonate need close monitoring.
Acidosis is often milder and potassium may be high rather than low (type 4 pattern); weakness and cramps are less prominent.

key_questions.question: When did the weakness and tiredness start, and has it been getting worse?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual onset over weeks to months, slowly progressive; a chronic course points to a tubular disorder rather than an acute cause of acidosis

key_questions.question: Have you been drinking and urinating much more than usual?
key_questions.looking_for: Thirst and polyuria from the concentrating defect and potassium loss; supports a renal tubular cause

key_questions.question: Have you ever passed a kidney stone or been told you have calcium in your kidneys?
key_questions.looking_for: Recurrent stones or nephrocalcinosis, which strongly favors distal (type 1) RTA

key_questions.question: Do your muscles feel weak or cramp, and is it hard to climb stairs or get out of a chair?
key_questions.looking_for: Proximal muscle weakness and cramps from hypokalemia; severity tracks the potassium level

key_questions.question: Have you had any bone pain, fractures, or in a child, trouble growing or bowing of the legs?
key_questions.looking_for: Bone pain, fractures, rickets or growth failure from chronic acidosis and phosphate loss

key_questions.question: Have you had a lot of watery diarrhea, or used laxatives?
key_questions.looking_for: Profuse diarrhea or laxative misuse causes the same normal-anion-gap acidosis and must be excluded

key_questions.question: Do you take topiramate, acetazolamide, or any diuretic?
key_questions.looking_for: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors and diuretics cause or worsen a renal tubular acidosis

key_questions.question: Have you ever been given amphotericin B or ifosfamide, or taken high doses of ibuprofen?
key_questions.looking_for: Drugs that injure the tubules and cause a secondary RTA

key_questions.question: Do you have dry eyes or dry mouth, joint pain or rashes?
key_questions.looking_for: Sjögren syndrome or another autoimmune disease, a common adult cause of distal RTA

key_questions.question: Has anyone in your family had kidney problems, kidney stones, or hearing loss in childhood?
key_questions.looking_for: Inherited tubulopathy or familial RTA, especially in a child

key_questions.question: Do you have sickle cell disease or a history of chronic kidney disease?
key_questions.looking_for: Conditions that cause a secondary tubular or type 4 pattern

key_questions.question: Have you had palpitations, or any numbness or tingling in your hands and feet?
key_questions.looking_for: Cardiac irritability and paresthesias from hypokalemia; suggests more severe potassium depletion

key_questions.question: Have you had vomiting, or a recent severe illness or infection?
key_questions.looking_for: Vomiting and acute illness cause a different pattern of acidosis and argue against a chronic tubular cause

key_questions.question: Do you drink alcohol heavily, or use any solvents or inhalants?
key_questions.looking_for: Toluene exposure and alcohol-related ketoacidosis as alternative causes of acidosis

accepted_names: Hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis due to renal tubular acidosis
reasoning_points: A normal-anion-gap (hyperchloremic) metabolic acidosis with low serum bicarbonate and high chloride
An inappropriately alkaline urine (pH above 5.5) during systemic acidosis, the hallmark of distal RTA
Hypokalemia in types 1 and 2, or hyperkalemia in type 4
A positive urine anion gap or failure to acidify the urine after an acid load confirming impaired distal ammonium excretion
A fractional bicarbonate excretion above 15% after loading indicating proximal (type 2) RTA
Non-renal bicarbonate loss such as profuse diarrhea or laxative use excluded
Advanced kidney failure excluded as the cause of the acidosis
Associated features such as nephrocalcinosis, kidney stones, rickets or growth failure in children
An underlying cause sought, especially autoimmune disease such as Sjögren syndrome in adults, or an offending medication

easy: Adult with chronic fatigue, muscle weakness and cramps
Low bicarbonate with a normal anion gap and high chloride
Hypokalemia with an inappropriately alkaline urine pH
Recurrent kidney stones or nephrocalcinosis on imaging
medium: Child with failure to thrive, vomiting and bow legs rather than stones
Adult with dry eyes and dry mouth suggesting Sjögren syndrome
Patient on topiramate or acetazolamide with a new normal-anion-gap acidosis
Mild acidosis found incidentally on routine labs with few symptoms
hard: Older adult whose bone pain and mild acidosis are attributed to aging
Pregnant patient whose nausea and vomiting mask the acidosis
Patient with chronic kidney disease where the acidosis is mild and the potassium is high rather than low (type 4 pattern)
Mixed disorder with a normal pH despite low bicarbonate, requiring careful acid-base interpretation
Distinguishing proximal from distal RTA when the urine pH is equivocal
